163|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
164|    | expr         | value   | reason                                        |
165|    +==============+=========+===============================================+
166|    | z**0         | 1       | Although arguments over 0**0 exist, see [2].  |
167|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
168|    | z**1         | z       |                                               |
169|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
170|    | (-oo)**(-1)  | 0       |                                               |
171|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
172|    | (-1)**-1     | -1      |                                               |
173|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
174|    | S.Zero**-1   | zoo     | This is not strictly true, as 0**-1 may be    |
175|    |              |         | undefined, but is convenient in some contexts |
176|    |              |         | where the base is assumed to be positive.     |
177|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
178|    | 1**-1        | 1       |                                               |
179|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
180|    | oo**-1       | 0       |                                               |
181|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
182|    | 0**oo        | 0       | Because for all complex numbers z near        |
183|    |              |         | 0, z**oo -> 0.                                |
184|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
185|    | 0**-oo       | zoo     | This is not strictly true, as 0**oo may be    |
186|    |              |         | oscillating between positive and negative     |
187|    |              |         | values or rotating in the complex plane.      |
188|    |              |         | It is convenient, however, when the base      |
189|    |              |         | is positive.                                  |
190|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
191|    | 1**oo        | nan     | Because there are various cases where         |
192|    | 1**-oo       |         | lim(x(t),t)=1, lim(y(t),t)=oo (or -oo),       |
193|    |              |         | but lim( x(t)**y(t), t) != 1.  See [3].       |
194|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
195|    | b**zoo       | nan     | Because b**z has no limit as z -> zoo         |
196|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
197|    | (-1)**oo     | nan     | Because of oscillations in the limit.         |
198|    | (-1)**(-oo)  |         |                                               |
199|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
200|    | oo**oo       | oo      |                                               |
201|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
202|    | oo**-oo      | 0       |                                               |
203|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+
204|    | (-oo)**oo    | nan     |                                               |
205|    | (-oo)**-oo   |         |                                               |
206|    +--------------+---------+-----------------------------------------------+

829|        b = self.base
830|        e = self.exp
831|        if not b.is_Mul:
832|            return self
833|
834|        cargs, nc = b.args_cnc(split_1=False)
835|

837|        # expansion but we have to watch out for things
838|        # that don't have an _eval_expand method
839|        if nc:
840|            nc = [i._eval_expand_power_base(**hints)
841|                if hasattr(i, '_eval_expand_power_base') else i
842|                for i in nc]
843|
844|            if e.is_Integer:
845|                if e.is_positive:
846|                    rv = Mul(*nc*e)
847|                else:
848|                    rv = 1/Mul(*nc*-e)
849|                if cargs:
850|                    rv *= Mul(*cargs)**e
851|                return rv
852|
853|            if not cargs:
854|                return self.func(Mul(*nc), e, evaluate=False)
855|
856|            nc = [Mul(*nc)]
857|
858|        # sift the commutative bases
859|        other, maybe_real = sift(cargs, lambda x: x.is_real is False,
860|            binary=True)
861|        def pred(x):
862|            if x is S.ImaginaryUnit:
863|                return S.ImaginaryUnit
864|            polar = x.is_polar
865|            if polar:
866|                return True
867|            if polar is None:
868|                return fuzzy_bool(x.is_nonnegative)
869|        sifted = sift(maybe_real, pred)
870|        nonneg = sifted[True]
871|        other += sifted[None]
872|        neg = sifted[False]
873|        imag = sifted[S.ImaginaryUnit]
874|        if imag:
875|            I = S.ImaginaryUnit
876|            i = len(imag) % 4
877|            if i == 0:
878|                pass
879|            elif i == 1:
880|                other.append(I)
881|            elif i == 2:
882|                if neg:
883|                    nonn = -neg.pop()
884|                    if nonn is not S.One:
885|                        nonneg.append(nonn)
886|                else:
887|                    neg.append(S.NegativeOne)
888|            else:
889|                if neg:
890|                    nonn = -neg.pop()
891|                    if nonn is not S.One:
892|                        nonneg.append(nonn)
893|                else:
894|                    neg.append(S.NegativeOne)

896|            del imag

899|

902|            cargs = nonneg + neg + other
903|            other = nc

907|            # no automatic expansion is done
908|
909|            assert not e.is_Integer

911|            # handle negatives by making them all positive and putting

915|                if not other and neg[0].is_Number:

930|                other.extend(neg)

932|
933|            cargs = nonneg
934|            other += nc

937|        if cargs:
938|            rv *= Mul(*[self.func(b, e, evaluate=False) for b in cargs])
939|        if other:
940|            rv *= self.func(Mul(*other), e, evaluate=False)

983|                    if n == 2:

991|                    # where 'a' and 'b' are real numbers and 'n' is integer.
992|                    a, b = base.as_real_imag()

363|    def unify(f, g):
364|        """
365|        Make ``f`` and ``g`` belong to the same domain.
366|
367|        Examples
368|        ========
369|
370|        >>> from sympy import Poly

372|
373|        >>> f, g = Poly(x/2 + 1), Poly(2*x + 1)

375|        >>> f
376|        Poly(1/2*x + 1, x, domain='QQ')
377|        >>> g
378|        Poly(2*x + 1, x, domain='ZZ')
379|
380|        >>> F, G = f.unify(g)
381|
382|        >>> F
383|        Poly(1/2*x + 1, x, domain='QQ')
384|        >>> G
385|        Poly(2*x + 1, x, domain='QQ')
386|
387|        """
388|        _, per, F, G = f._unify(g)

391|    def _unify(f, g):
392|        g = sympify(g)
393|
394|        if not g.is_Poly:
395|            try:
396|                return f.rep.dom, f.per, f.rep, f.rep.per(f.rep.dom.from_sympy(g))
397|            except CoercionFailed:
398|                raise UnificationFailed("can't unify %s with %s" % (f, g))
399|
400|        if isinstance(f.rep, DMP) and isinstance(g.rep, DMP):
401|            gens = _unify_gens(f.gens, g.gens)
402|
403|            dom, lev = f.rep.dom.unify(g.rep.dom, gens), len(gens) - 1
404|
405|            if f.gens != gens:
406|                f_monoms, f_coeffs = _dict_reorder(
407|                    f.rep.to_dict(), f.gens, gens)
408|
409|                if f.rep.dom != dom:
410|                    f_coeffs = [dom.convert(c, f.rep.dom) for c in f_coeffs]
411|
412|                F = DMP(dict(list(zip(f_monoms, f_coeffs))), dom, lev)
413|            else:
414|                F = f.rep.convert(dom)
415|
416|            if g.gens != gens:
417|                g_monoms, g_coeffs = _dict_reorder(
418|                    g.rep.to_dict(), g.gens, gens)
419|
420|                if g.rep.dom != dom:
421|                    g_coeffs = [dom.convert(c, g.rep.dom) for c in g_coeffs]
422|
423|                G = DMP(dict(list(zip(g_monoms, g_coeffs))), dom, lev)
424|            else:
425|                G = g.rep.convert(dom)
426|        else:
427|            raise UnificationFailed("can't unify %s with %s" % (f, g))
428|
429|        cls = f.__class__
430|
431|        def per(rep, dom=dom, gens=gens, remove=None):
432|            if remove is not None:
433|                gens = gens[:remove] + gens[remove + 1:]
434|
435|                if not gens:
436|                    return dom.to_sympy(rep)
437|
438|            return cls.new(rep, *gens)
439|
440|        return dom, per, F, G

615|        """
616|        Remove dummy generators from ``f`` that are to the left of
617|        specified ``gen`` in the generators as ordered. When ``gen``
618|        is an integer, it refers to the generator located at that
619|        position within the tuple of generators of ``f``.

640|            if any(i for i in monom[:j]):

642|                raise PolynomialError("can't left trim %s" % f)

644|            terms[monom[j:]] = coeff

2613|    def dispersionset(f, g=None):
2614|        r"""Compute the *dispersion set* of two polynomials.
2615|
2616|        For two polynomials `f(x)` and `g(x)` with `\deg f > 0`
2617|        and `\deg g > 0` the dispersion set `\operatorname{J}(f, g)` is defined as:
2618|
2619|        .. math::
2620|            \operatorname{J}(f, g)
2621|            & := \{a \in \mathbb{N}_0 | \gcd(f(x), g(x+a)) \neq 1\} \\
2622|            &  = \{a \in \mathbb{N}_0 | \deg \gcd(f(x), g(x+a)) \geq 1\}
2623|
2624|        For a single polynomial one defines `\operatorname{J}(f) := \operatorname{J}(f, f)`.
2625|
2626|        Examples
2627|        ========
2628|
2629|        >>> from sympy import poly
2630|        >>> from sympy.polys.dispersion import dispersion, dispersionset
2631|        >>> from sympy.abc import x
2632|
2633|        Dispersion set and dispersion of a simple polynomial:
2634|
2635|        >>> fp = poly((x - 3)*(x + 3), x)
2636|        >>> sorted(dispersionset(fp))
2637|        [0, 6]
2638|        >>> dispersion(fp)
2639|        6
2640|
2641|        Note that the definition of the dispersion is not symmetric:
2642|
2643|        >>> fp = poly(x**4 - 3*x**2 + 1, x)
2644|        >>> gp = fp.shift(-3)
2645|        >>> sorted(dispersionset(fp, gp))
2646|        [2, 3, 4]
2647|        >>> dispersion(fp, gp)
2648|        4
2649|        >>> sorted(dispersionset(gp, fp))
2650|        []
2651|        >>> dispersion(gp, fp)
2652|        -oo
2653|
2654|        Computing the dispersion also works over field extensions:
2655|
2656|        >>> from sympy import sqrt
2657|        >>> fp = poly(x**2 + sqrt(5)*x - 1, x, domain='QQ<sqrt(5)>')
2658|        >>> gp = poly(x**2 + (2 + sqrt(5))*x + sqrt(5), x, domain='QQ<sqrt(5)>')
2659|        >>> sorted(dispersionset(fp, gp))
2660|        [2]
2661|        >>> sorted(dispersionset(gp, fp))
2662|        [1, 4]
2663|
2664|        We can even perform the computations for polynomials
2665|        having symbolic coefficients:
2666|
2667|        >>> from sympy.abc import a
2668|        >>> fp = poly(4*x**4 + (4*a + 8)*x**3 + (a**2 + 6*a + 4)*x**2 + (a**2 + 2*a)*x, x)
2669|        >>> sorted(dispersionset(fp))
2670|        [0, 1]
2671|
2672|        See Also
2673|        ========
2674|
2675|        dispersion
2676|
2677|        References
2678|        ==========
2679|
2680|        1. [ManWright94]_
2681|        2. [Koepf98]_
2682|        3. [Abramov71]_
2683|        4. [Man93]_
2684|        """
2685|        from sympy.polys.dispersion import dispersionset
2686|        return dispersionset(f, g)

2697|            &  = \max\{ \{a \in \mathbb{N} | \gcd(f(x), g(x+a)) \neq 1\} \cup \{0\} \}

2699|        and for a single polynomial `\operatorname{dis}(f) := \operatorname{dis}(f, f)`.

2702|        ========

2706|        >>> from sympy.abc import x

3278|    def intervals(f, all=False, eps=None, inf=None, sup=None, fast=False, sqf=False):
3279|        """
3280|        Compute isolating intervals for roots of ``f``.
3281|
3282|        For real roots the Vincent-Akritas-Strzebonski (VAS) continued fractions method is used.
3283|
3284|        References:
3285|        ===========
3286|           1. Alkiviadis G. Akritas and Adam W. Strzebonski: A Comparative Study of Two Real Root
3287|           Isolation Methods . Nonlinear Analysis: Modelling and Control, Vol. 10, No. 4, 297-304, 2005.
3288|           2. Alkiviadis G. Akritas, Adam W. Strzebonski and Panagiotis S. Vigklas: Improving the
3289|           Performance of the Continued Fractions Method Using new Bounds of Positive Roots. Nonlinear
3290|           Analysis: Modelling and Control, Vol. 13, No. 3, 265-279, 2008.
3291|
3292|        Examples
3293|        ========
3294|
3295|        >>> from sympy import Poly
3296|        >>> from sympy.abc import x
3297|
3298|        >>> Poly(x**2 - 3, x).intervals()
3299|        [((-2, -1), 1), ((1, 2), 1)]
3300|        >>> Poly(x**2 - 3, x).intervals(eps=1e-2)
3301|        [((-26/15, -19/11), 1), ((19/11, 26/15), 1)]
3302|
3303|        """
3304|        if eps is not None:
3305|            eps = QQ.convert(eps)
3306|
3307|            if eps <= 0:
3308|                raise ValueError("'eps' must be a positive rational")
3309|
3310|        if inf is not None:
3311|            inf = QQ.convert(inf)
3312|        if sup is not None:
3313|            sup = QQ.convert(sup)
3314|
3315|        if hasattr(f.rep, 'intervals'):
3316|            result = f.rep.intervals(
3317|                all=all, eps=eps, inf=inf, sup=sup, fast=fast, sqf=sqf)
3318|        else:  # pragma: no cover
3319|            raise OperationNotSupported(f, 'intervals')
3320|
3321|        if sqf:
3322|            def _real(interval):
3323|                s, t = interval
3324|                return (QQ.to_sympy(s), QQ.to_sympy(t))
3325|
3326|            if not all:
3327|                return list(map(_real, result))
3328|
3329|            def _complex(rectangle):
3330|                (u, v), (s, t) = rectangle
3331|                return (QQ.to_sympy(u) + I*QQ.to_sympy(v),
3332|                        QQ.to_sympy(s) + I*QQ.to_sympy(t))
3333|
3334|            real_part, complex_part = result
3335|
3336|            return list(map(_real, real_part)), list(map(_complex, complex_part))
3337|        else:
3338|            def _real(interval):
3339|                (s, t), k = interval
3340|                return ((QQ.to_sympy(s), QQ.to_sympy(t)), k)
3341|
3342|            if not all:
3343|                return list(map(_real, result))
3344|
3345|            def _complex(rectangle):
3346|                ((u, v), (s, t)), k = rectangle
3347|                return ((QQ.to_sympy(u) + I*QQ.to_sympy(v),
3348|                         QQ.to_sympy(s) + I*QQ.to_sympy(t)), k)
3349|
3350|            real_part, complex_part = result
3351|
3352|            return list(map(_real, real_part)), list(map(_complex, complex_part))

3531|    def nroots(f, n=15, maxsteps=50, cleanup=True):
3532|        """
3533|        Compute numerical approximations of roots of ``f``.
3534|
3535|        Parameters
3536|        ==========
3537|
3538|        n ... the number of digits to calculate
3539|        maxsteps ... the maximum number of iterations to do
3540|
3541|        If the accuracy `n` cannot be reached in `maxsteps`, it will raise an
3542|        exception. You need to rerun with higher maxsteps.
3543|
3544|        Examples
3545|        ========
3546|
3547|        >>> from sympy import Poly
3548|        >>> from sympy.abc import x
3549|
3550|        >>> Poly(x**2 - 3).nroots(n=15)
3551|        [-1.73205080756888, 1.73205080756888]
3552|        >>> Poly(x**2 - 3).nroots(n=30)
3553|        [-1.73205080756887729352744634151, 1.73205080756887729352744634151]
3554|
3555|        """
3556|        if f.is_multivariate:
3557|            raise MultivariatePolynomialError(
3558|                "can't compute numerical roots of %s" % f)
3559|
3560|        if f.degree() <= 0:
3561|            return []
3562|
3563|        # For integer and rational coefficients, convert them to integers only
3564|        # (for accuracy). Otherwise just try to convert the coefficients to
3565|        # mpmath.mpc and raise an exception if the conversion fails.
3566|        if f.rep.dom is ZZ:
3567|            coeffs = [int(coeff) for coeff in f.all_coeffs()]
3568|        elif f.rep.dom is QQ:
3569|            denoms = [coeff.q for coeff in f.all_coeffs()]
3570|            from sympy.core.numbers import ilcm
3571|            fac = ilcm(*denoms)
3572|            coeffs = [int(coeff*fac) for coeff in f.all_coeffs()]
3573|        else:
3574|            coeffs = [coeff.evalf(n=n).as_real_imag()
3575|                    for coeff in f.all_coeffs()]
3576|            try:
3577|                coeffs = [mpmath.mpc(*coeff) for coeff in coeffs]
3578|            except TypeError:
3579|                raise DomainError("Numerical domain expected, got %s" % \
3580|                        f.rep.dom)
3581|
3582|        dps = mpmath.mp.dps
3583|        mpmath.mp.dps = n
3584|
3585|        try:
3586|            # We need to add extra precision to guard against losing accuracy.
3587|            # 10 times the degree of the polynomial seems to work well.
3588|            roots = mpmath.polyroots(coeffs, maxsteps=maxsteps,
3589|                    cleanup=cleanup, error=False, extraprec=f.degree()*10)
3590|
3591|            # Mpmath puts real roots first, then complex ones (as does all_roots)
3592|            # so we make sure this convention holds here, too.
3593|            roots = list(map(sympify,
3594|                sorted(roots, key=lambda r: (1 if r.imag else 0, r.real, r.imag))))
3595|        except NoConvergence:
3596|            raise NoConvergence(
3597|                'convergence to root failed; try n < %s or maxsteps > %s' % (
3598|                n, maxsteps))
3599|        finally:
3600|            mpmath.mp.dps = dps
3601|
3602|        return roots

3604|    def ground_roots(f):
3605|        """
3606|        Compute roots of ``f`` by factorization in the ground domain.
3607|
3608|        Examples
3609|        ========
3610|
3611|        >>> from sympy import Poly
3612|        >>> from sympy.abc import x
3613|
3614|        >>> Poly(x**6 - 4*x**4 + 4*x**3 - x**2).ground_roots()

3618|        if f.is_multivariate:

3621|
3622|        roots = {}
3623|

389|    def _print_Mul(self, expr):
390|        from sympy.core.power import Pow
391|        from sympy.physics.units import Quantity
392|        include_parens = False
393|        if _coeff_isneg(expr):
394|            expr = -expr
395|            tex = "- "
396|            if expr.is_Add:
397|                tex += "("
398|                include_parens = True
399|        else:
400|            tex = ""
401|
402|        from sympy.simplify import fraction
403|        numer, denom = fraction(expr, exact=True)
404|        separator = self._settings['mul_symbol_latex']
405|        numbersep = self._settings['mul_symbol_latex_numbers']
406|
407|        def convert(expr):
408|            if not expr.is_Mul:
409|                return str(self._print(expr))
410|            else:
411|                _tex = last_term_tex = ""
412|
413|                if self.order not in ('old', 'none'):
414|                    args = expr.as_ordered_factors()
415|                else:
416|                    args = list(expr.args)
417|
418|                # If quantities are present append them at the back
419|                args = sorted(args, key=lambda x: isinstance(x, Quantity) or
420|                             (isinstance(x, Pow) and isinstance(x.base, Quantity)))
421|
422|                for i, term in enumerate(args):
423|                    term_tex = self._print(term)
424|
425|                    if self._needs_mul_brackets(term, first=(i == 0),
426|                                                last=(i == len(args) - 1)):
427|                        term_tex = r"\left(%s\right)" % term_tex
428|
429|                    if _between_two_numbers_p[0].search(last_term_tex) and \
430|                            _between_two_numbers_p[1].match(term_tex):
431|                        # between two numbers
432|                        _tex += numbersep
433|                    elif _tex:
434|                        _tex += separator
435|
436|                    _tex += term_tex
437|                    last_term_tex = term_tex
438|                return _tex
439|
440|        if denom is S.One and Pow(1, -1, evaluate=False) not in expr.args:
441|            # use the original expression here, since fraction() may have
442|            # altered it when producing numer and denom
443|            tex += convert(expr)
444|
445|        else:
446|            snumer = convert(numer)
447|            sdenom = convert(denom)
448|            ldenom = len(sdenom.split())
449|            ratio = self._settings['long_frac_ratio']
450|            if self._settings['fold_short_frac'] \
451|                   and ldenom <= 2 and not "^" in sdenom:
452|                # handle short fractions
453|                if self._needs_mul_brackets(numer, last=False):
454|                    tex += r"\left(%s\right) / %s" % (snumer, sdenom)
455|                else:
456|                    tex += r"%s / %s" % (snumer, sdenom)
457|            elif ratio is not None and \
458|                    len(snumer.split()) > ratio*ldenom:
459|                # handle long fractions
460|                if self._needs_mul_brackets(numer, last=True):
461|                    tex += r"\frac{1}{%s}%s\left(%s\right)" \
462|                        % (sdenom, separator, snumer)
463|                elif numer.is_Mul:
464|                    # split a long numerator
465|                    a = S.One
466|                    b = S.One
467|                    for x in numer.args:
468|                        if self._needs_mul_brackets(x, last=False) or \
469|                                len(convert(a*x).split()) > ratio*ldenom or \
470|                                (b.is_commutative is x.is_commutative is False):
471|                            b *= x
472|                        else:
473|                            a *= x
474|                    if self._needs_mul_brackets(b, last=True):
475|                        tex += r"\frac{%s}{%s}%s\left(%s\right)" \
476|                            % (convert(a), sdenom, separator, convert(b))
477|                    else:
478|                        tex += r"\frac{%s}{%s}%s%s" \
479|                            % (convert(a), sdenom, separator, convert(b))
480|                else:
481|                    tex += r"\frac{1}{%s}%s%s" % (sdenom, separator, snumer)
482|            else:
483|                tex += r"\frac{%s}{%s}" % (snumer, sdenom)
484|
485|        if include_parens:
486|            tex += ")"
487|        return tex

489|    def _print_Pow(self, expr):
490|        # Treat x**Rational(1,n) as special case
491|        if expr.exp.is_Rational and abs(expr.exp.p) == 1 and expr.exp.q != 1:
492|            base = self._print(expr.base)
493|            expq = expr.exp.q
494|
495|            if expq == 2:
496|                tex = r"\sqrt{%s}" % base
497|            elif self._settings['itex']:
498|                tex = r"\root{%d}{%s}" % (expq, base)
499|            else:
500|                tex = r"\sqrt[%d]{%s}" % (expq, base)
501|
502|            if expr.exp.is_negative:
503|                return r"\frac{1}{%s}" % tex
504|            else:
505|                return tex
506|        elif self._settings['fold_frac_powers'] \
507|            and expr.exp.is_Rational \
508|                and expr.exp.q != 1:
509|            base, p, q = self.parenthesize(expr.base, PRECEDENCE['Pow']), expr.exp.p, expr.exp.q
510|            # issue #12886: add parentheses for superscripts raised to powers
511|            if '^' in base and expr.base.is_Symbol:
512|                base = r"\left(%s\right)" % base
513|            if expr.base.is_Function:
514|                return self._print(expr.base, exp="%s/%s" % (p, q))
515|            return r"%s^{%s/%s}" % (base, p, q)
516|        elif expr.exp.is_Rational and expr.exp.is_negative and expr.base.is_commutative:
517|            # special case for 1^(-x), issue 9216
518|            if expr.base == 1:
519|                return r"%s^{%s}" % (expr.base, expr.exp)
520|            # things like 1/x
521|            return self._print_Mul(expr)
522|        else:
523|            if expr.base.is_Function:
524|                return self._print(expr.base, exp=self._print(expr.exp))
525|            else:
526|                tex = r"%s^{%s}"
527|                exp = self._print(expr.exp)
528|                # issue #12886: add parentheses around superscripts raised to powers
529|                base = self.parenthesize(expr.base, PRECEDENCE['Pow'])
530|                if '^' in base and expr.base.is_Symbol:
531|                    base = r"\left(%s\right)" % base
532|                elif isinstance(expr.base, Derivative
533|                        ) and base.startswith(r'\left('
534|                        ) and re.match(r'\\left\(\\d?d?dot', base
535|                        ) and base.endswith(r'\right)'):
536|                    # don't use parentheses around dotted derivative
537|                    base = base[6: -7]  # remove outermost added parens
538|
539|                return tex % (base, exp)

698|    def _hprint_Function(self, func):
699|        r'''
700|        Logic to decide how to render a function to latex
701|          - if it is a recognized latex name, use the appropriate latex command
702|          - if it is a single letter, just use that letter
703|          - if it is a longer name, then put \operatorname{} around it and be
704|            mindful of undercores in the name
705|        '''
706|        func = self._deal_with_super_sub(func)
707|        if func in accepted_latex_functions:
708|            name = r"\%s" % func
709|        elif len(func) == 1 or func.startswith('\\'):
710|            name = func
711|        else:
712|            name = r"\operatorname{%s}" % func
713|        return name

715|    def _print_Function(self, expr, exp=None):
716|        r'''
717|        Render functions to LaTeX, handling functions that LaTeX knows about
718|        e.g., sin, cos, ... by using the proper LaTeX command (\sin, \cos, ...).
719|        For single-letter function names, render them as regular LaTeX math
720|        symbols. For multi-letter function names that LaTeX does not know
721|        about, (e.g., Li, sech) use \operatorname{} so that the function name
722|        is rendered in Roman font and LaTeX handles spacing properly.
723|
724|        expr is the expression involving the function
725|        exp is an exponent
726|        '''
727|        func = expr.func.__name__
728|        if hasattr(self, '_print_' + func) and \
729|            not isinstance(expr.func, UndefinedFunction):
730|            return getattr(self, '_print_' + func)(expr, exp)
731|        else:
732|            args = [ str(self._print(arg)) for arg in expr.args ]
733|            # How inverse trig functions should be displayed, formats are:
734|            # abbreviated: asin, full: arcsin, power: sin^-1
735|            inv_trig_style = self._settings['inv_trig_style']
736|            # If we are dealing with a power-style inverse trig function
737|            inv_trig_power_case = False
738|            # If it is applicable to fold the argument brackets
739|            can_fold_brackets = self._settings['fold_func_brackets'] and \
740|                len(args) == 1 and \
741|                not self._needs_function_brackets(expr.args[0])
742|
743|            inv_trig_table = ["asin", "acos", "atan", "acsc", "asec", "acot"]
744|
745|            # If the function is an inverse trig function, handle the style
746|            if func in inv_trig_table:
747|                if inv_trig_style == "abbreviated":
748|                    func = func
749|                elif inv_trig_style == "full":
750|                    func = "arc" + func[1:]
751|                elif inv_trig_style == "power":
752|                    func = func[1:]
753|                    inv_trig_power_case = True
754|
755|                    # Can never fold brackets if we're raised to a power
756|                    if exp is not None:
757|                        can_fold_brackets = False
758|
759|            if inv_trig_power_case:
760|                if func in accepted_latex_functions:
761|                    name = r"\%s^{-1}" % func
762|                else:
763|                    name = r"\operatorname{%s}^{-1}" % func
764|            elif exp is not None:
765|                name = r'%s^{%s}' % (self._hprint_Function(func), exp)
766|            else:
767|                name = self._hprint_Function(func)
768|
769|            if can_fold_brackets:
770|                if func in accepted_latex_functions:
771|                    # Wrap argument safely to avoid parse-time conflicts
772|                    # with the function name itself
773|                    name += r" {%s}"
774|                else:
775|                    name += r"%s"
776|            else:
777|                name += r"{\left (%s \right )}"
778|
779|            if inv_trig_power_case and exp is not None:
780|                name += r"^{%s}" % exp
781|
782|            return name % ",".join(args)

### GitHub Problem Description ###
Lambdify misinterprets some matrix expressions
Using lambdify on an expression containing an identity matrix gives us an unexpected result:

```python
>>> import numpy as np
>>> n = symbols('n', integer=True)
>>> A = MatrixSymbol("A", n, n)
>>> a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
>>> f = lambdify(A, A + Identity(n))
>>> f(a)
array([[1.+1.j, 2.+1.j],
       [3.+1.j, 4.+1.j]])
```

Instead, the output should be  `array([[2, 2], [3, 5]])`, since we're adding an identity matrix to the array. Inspecting the globals and source code of `f` shows us why we get the result:

```python
>>> import inspect
>>> print(inspect.getsource(f))
def _lambdifygenerated(A):
    return (I + A)
>>> f.__globals__['I']
1j
```

The code printer prints `I`, which is currently being interpreted as a Python built-in complex number. The printer should support printing identity matrices, and signal an error for unsupported expressions that might be misinterpreted.

284|    How it works
285|    ============
286|
287|    When using this function, it helps a great deal to have an idea of what it
288|    is doing. At its core, lambdify is nothing more than a namespace
289|    translation, on top of a special printer that makes some corner cases work

291|
292|    To understand lambdify, first we must properly understand how Python
293|    namespaces work. Say we had two files. One called ``sin_cos_sympy.py``,
294|    with
295|
296|    .. code:: python
297|
298|        # sin_cos_sympy.py
299|
300|        from sympy import sin, cos
301|
302|        def sin_cos(x):
303|            return sin(x) + cos(x)
304|
305|
306|    and one called ``sin_cos_numpy.py`` with
307|
308|    .. code:: python
309|
310|        # sin_cos_numpy.py
311|
312|        from numpy import sin, cos
313|
314|        def sin_cos(x):
315|            return sin(x) + cos(x)
316|
317|    The two files define an identical function ``sin_cos``. However, in the
318|    first file, ``sin`` and ``cos`` are defined as the SymPy ``sin`` and
319|    ``cos``. In the second, they are defined as the NumPy versions.
320|
321|    If we were to import the first file and use the ``sin_cos`` function, we
322|    would get something like
323|
324|    >>> from sin_cos_sympy import sin_cos # doctest: +SKIP
325|    >>> sin_cos(1) # doctest: +SKIP
326|    cos(1) + sin(1)
327|
328|    On the other hand, if we imported ``sin_cos`` from the second file, we
329|    would get
330|
331|    >>> from sin_cos_numpy import sin_cos # doctest: +SKIP
332|    >>> sin_cos(1) # doctest: +SKIP
333|    1.38177329068
334|
335|    In the first case we got a symbolic output, because it used the symbolic
336|    ``sin`` and ``cos`` functions from SymPy. In the second, we got a numeric
337|    result, because ``sin_cos`` used the numeric ``sin`` and ``cos`` functions
338|    from NumPy. But notice that the versions of ``sin`` and ``cos`` that were
339|    used was not inherent to the ``sin_cos`` function definition. Both
340|    ``sin_cos`` definitions are exactly the same. Rather, it was based on the
341|    names defined at the module where the ``sin_cos`` function was defined.
342|
343|    The key point here is that when function in Python references a name that
344|    is not defined in the function, that name is looked up in the "global"
345|    namespace of the module where that function is defined.
346|
347|    Now, in Python, we can emulate this behavior without actually writing a
348|    file to disk using the ``exec`` function. ``exec`` takes a string
349|    containing a block of Python code, and a dictionary that should contain
350|    the global variables of the module. It then executes the code "in" that
351|    dictionary, as if it were the module globals. The following is equivalent
352|    to the ``sin_cos`` defined in ``sin_cos_sympy.py``:
353|
354|    >>> import sympy
355|    >>> module_dictionary = {'sin': sympy.sin, 'cos': sympy.cos}
356|    >>> exec('''
357|    ... def sin_cos(x):
358|    ...     return sin(x) + cos(x)
359|    ... ''', module_dictionary)
360|    >>> sin_cos = module_dictionary['sin_cos']
361|    >>> sin_cos(1)
362|    cos(1) + sin(1)

364|    and similarly with ``sin_cos_numpy``:
365|
366|    >>> import numpy
367|    >>> module_dictionary = {'sin': numpy.sin, 'cos': numpy.cos}
368|    >>> exec('''
369|    ... def sin_cos(x):
370|    ...     return sin(x) + cos(x)
371|    ... ''', module_dictionary)
372|    >>> sin_cos = module_dictionary['sin_cos']
373|    >>> sin_cos(1)
374|    1.38177329068

376|    So now we can get an idea of how ``lambdify`` works. The name "lambdify"
377|    comes from the fact that we can think of something like ``lambdify(x,
378|    sin(x) + cos(x), 'numpy')`` as ``lambda x: sin(x) + cos(x)``, where
379|    ``sin`` and ``cos`` come from the ``numpy`` namespace. This is also why
380|    the symbols argument is first in ``lambdify``, as opposed to most SymPy
381|    functions where it comes after the expression: to better mimic the
382|    ``lambda`` keyword.
383|
384|    ``lambdify`` takes the input expression (like ``sin(x) + cos(x)``) and
385|
386|    1. Converts it to a string
387|    2. Creates a module globals dictionary based on the modules that are
388|       passed in (by default, it uses the NumPy module)
389|    3. Creates the string ``"def func({vars}): return {expr}"``, where ``{vars}`` is the
390|       list of variables separated by commas, and ``{expr}`` is the string
391|       created in step 1., then ``exec``s that string with the module globals
392|       namespace and returns ``func``.
393|
394|    In fact, functions returned by ``lambdify`` support inspection. So you can
395|    see exactly how they are defined by using ``inspect.getsource``, or ``??`` if you
396|    are using IPython or the Jupyter notebook.
397|
398|    >>> f = lambdify(x, sin(x) + cos(x))
399|    >>> import inspect
400|    >>> print(inspect.getsource(f))
401|    def _lambdifygenerated(x):
402|        return (sin(x) + cos(x))
403|
404|    This shows us the source code of the function, but not the namespace it
405|    was defined in. We can inspect that by looking at the ``__globals__``
406|    attribute of ``f``:
407|
408|    >>> f.__globals__['sin']
409|    <ufunc 'sin'>
410|    >>> f.__globals__['cos']
411|    <ufunc 'cos'>
412|    >>> f.__globals__['sin'] is numpy.sin
413|    True
414|
415|    This shows us that ``sin`` and ``cos`` in the namespace of ``f`` will be
416|    ``numpy.sin`` and ``numpy.cos``.
417|
418|    Note that there are some convenience layers in each of these steps, but at
419|    the core, this is how ``lambdify`` works. Step 1 is done using the
420|    ``LambdaPrinter`` printers defined in the printing module (see
421|    :mod:`sympy.printing.lambdarepr`). This allows different SymPy expressions
422|    to define how they should be converted to a string for different modules.
423|    You can change which printer ``lambdify`` uses by passing a custom printer
424|    in to the ``printer`` argument.
425|
426|    Step 2 is augmented by certain translations. There are default
427|    translations for each module, but you can provide your own by passing a
428|    list to the ``modules`` argument. For instance,
429|
430|    >>> def mysin(x):
431|    ...     print('taking the sin of', x)
432|    ...     return numpy.sin(x)
433|    ...
434|    >>> f = lambdify(x, sin(x), [{'sin': mysin}, 'numpy'])
435|    >>> f(1)
436|    taking the sin of 1
437|    0.8414709848078965
438|
439|    The globals dictionary is generated from the list by merging the
440|    dictionary ``{'sin': mysin}`` and the module dictionary for NumPy. The
441|    merging is done so that earlier items take precedence, which is why
442|    ``mysin`` is used above instead of ``numpy.sin``.
443|
444|    If you want to modify the way ``lambdify`` works for a given function, it
445|    is usually easiest to do so by modifying the globals dictionary as such.
446|    In more complicated cases, it may be necessary to create and pass in a
447|    custom printer.
448|
449|    Finally, step 3 is augmented with certain convenience operations, such as
450|    the addition of a docstring.
451|
452|    Understanding how ``lambdify`` works can make it easier to avoid certain
453|    gotchas when using it. For instance, a common mistake is to create a
454|    lambdified function for one module (say, NumPy), and pass it objects from
455|    another (say, a SymPy expression).
456|
457|    For instance, say we create
458|
459|    >>> from sympy.abc import x
460|    >>> f = lambdify(x, x + 1, 'numpy')
461|
462|    Now if we pass in a NumPy array, we get that array plus 1
463|
464|    >>> import numpy
465|    >>> a = numpy.array([1, 2])
466|    >>> f(a)
467|    [2 3]
468|
469|    But what happens if you make the mistake of passing in a SymPy expression
470|    instead of a NumPy array:
471|
472|    >>> f(x + 1)
473|    x + 2
474|
475|    This worked, but it was only by accident. Now take a different lambdified
476|    function:
477|
478|    >>> from sympy import sin
479|    >>> g = lambdify(x, x + sin(x), 'numpy')
480|
481|    This works as expected on NumPy arrays:
482|
483|    >>> g(a)
484|    [1.84147098 2.90929743]
485|
486|    But if we try to pass in a SymPy expression, it fails
487|
488|    >>> g(x + 1)
489|    Traceback (most recent call last):
490|    ...
491|    AttributeError: 'Add' object has no attribute 'sin'
492|
493|    Now, let's look at what happened. The reason this fails is that ``g``
494|    calls ``numpy.sin`` on the input expression, and ``numpy.sin`` does not
495|    know how to operate on a SymPy object. **As a general rule, NumPy
496|    functions do not know how to operate on SymPy expressions, and SymPy
497|    functions do not know how to operate on NumPy arrays. This is why lambdify
498|    exists: to provide a bridge between SymPy and NumPy.**
499|
500|    However, why is it that ``f`` did work? That's because ``f`` doesn't call
501|    any functions, it only adds 1. So the resulting function that is created,
502|    ``def _lambdifygenerated(x): return x + 1`` does not depend on the globals
503|    namespace it is defined in. Thus it works, but only by accident. A future
504|    version of ``lambdify`` may remove this behavior.
505|
506|    Be aware that certain implementation details described here may change in
507|    future versions of SymPy. The API of passing in custom modules and
508|    printers will not change, but the details of how a lambda function is
509|    created may change. However, the basic idea will remain the same, and
510|    understanding it will be helpful to understanding the behavior of
511|    lambdify.
512|
513|    **In general: you should create lambdified functions for one module (say,
514|    NumPy), and only pass it input types that are compatible with that module
515|    (say, NumPy arrays).** Remember that by default, if the ``module``
516|    argument is not provided, ``lambdify`` creates functions using the NumPy
517|    and SciPy namespaces.
518|
519|    Examples
520|    ========
521|
522|    >>> from sympy.utilities.lambdify import implemented_function
523|    >>> from sympy import sqrt, sin, Matrix
524|    >>> from sympy import Function
525|    >>> from sympy.abc import w, x, y, z
526|
527|    >>> f = lambdify(x, x**2)
528|    >>> f(2)
529|    4
530|    >>> f = lambdify((x, y, z), [z, y, x])
531|    >>> f(1,2,3)
532|    [3, 2, 1]
533|    >>> f = lambdify(x, sqrt(x))
534|    >>> f(4)
535|    2.0
536|    >>> f = lambdify((x, y), sin(x*y)**2)
537|    >>> f(0, 5)
538|    0.0
539|    >>> row = lambdify((x, y), Matrix((x, x + y)).T, modules='sympy')
540|    >>> row(1, 2)
541|    Matrix([[1, 3]])
542|
543|    ``lambdify`` can be used to translate SymPy expressions into mpmath
544|    functions. This may be preferable to using ``evalf`` (which uses mpmath on
545|    the backend) in some cases.
546|
547|    >>> import mpmath
548|    >>> f = lambdify(x, sin(x), 'mpmath')
549|    >>> f(1)
550|    0.8414709848078965
551|
552|    Tuple arguments are handled and the lambdified function should
553|    be called with the same type of arguments as were used to create
554|    the function:
555|
556|    >>> f = lambdify((x, (y, z)), x + y)
557|    >>> f(1, (2, 4))
558|    3
559|
560|    The ``flatten`` function can be used to always work with flattened
561|    arguments:
562|
563|    >>> from sympy.utilities.iterables import flatten
564|    >>> args = w, (x, (y, z))
565|    >>> vals = 1, (2, (3, 4))
566|    >>> f = lambdify(flatten(args), w + x + y + z)
567|    >>> f(*flatten(vals))
568|    10
569|
570|    Functions present in ``expr`` can also carry their own numerical
571|    implementations, in a callable attached to the ``_imp_`` attribute. This
572|    can be used with undefined functions using the ``implemented_function``
573|    factory:
574|
575|    >>> f = implemented_function(Function('f'), lambda x: x+1)
576|    >>> func = lambdify(x, f(x))
577|    >>> func(4)
578|    5
579|
580|    ``lambdify`` always prefers ``_imp_`` implementations to implementations
581|    in other namespaces, unless the ``use_imps`` input parameter is False.
582|
583|    Usage with Tensorflow:
584|
585|    >>> import tensorflow as tf
586|    >>> from sympy import Max, sin
587|    >>> f = Max(x, sin(x))
588|    >>> func = lambdify(x, f, 'tensorflow')
589|    >>> result = func(tf.constant(1.0))
590|    >>> print(result) # a tf.Tensor representing the result of the calculation
591|    Tensor("Maximum:0", shape=(), dtype=float32)
592|    >>> sess = tf.Session()
593|    >>> sess.run(result) # compute result
594|    1.0
595|    >>> var = tf.Variable(1.0)
596|    >>> sess.run(tf.global_variables_initializer())
597|    >>> sess.run(func(var)) # also works for tf.Variable and tf.Placeholder
598|    1.0
599|    >>> tensor = tf.constant([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]]) # works with any shape tensor
600|    >>> sess.run(func(tensor))
601|    [[1. 2.]
602|     [3. 4.]]
603|
604|    Notes
605|    =====

608|      significant speedup over numpy. Please note that the available functions
609|      for numexpr are more limited than numpy but can be expanded with
610|      ``implemented_function`` and user defined subclasses of Function. If
611|      specified, numexpr may be the only option in modules. The official list

621|      >>> from sympy import lambdify, Matrix

645|      ZeroDivisionError: division by zero

654|
655|      >>> f = lambdify(x, Piecewise((x, x <= 1), (1/x, x > 1)), "math")

47|    coords : sequence of n-coordinate values. In the special
48|        case where n=2 or 3, a Point2D or Point3D will be created
49|        as appropriate.
50|    evaluate : if `True` (default), all floats are turn into
51|        exact types.
52|    dim : number of coordinates the point should have.  If coordinates
53|        are unspecified, they are padded with zeros.
54|    on_morph : indicates what should happen when the number of
55|        coordinates of a point need to be changed by adding or
56|        removing zeros.  Possible values are `'warn'`, `'error'`, or
57|        `ignore` (default).  No warning or error is given when `*args`
58|        is empty and `dim` is given. An error is always raised when
59|        trying to remove nonzero coordinates.
60|
61|
62|    Attributes
63|    ==========
64|
65|    length
66|    origin: A `Point` representing the origin of the
67|        appropriately-dimensioned space.

69|    Raises
70|    ======
71|
72|    TypeError : When instantiating with anything but a Point or sequence
73|    ValueError : when instantiating with a sequence with length < 2 or
74|        when trying to reduce dimensions if keyword `on_morph='error'` is
75|        set.

77|    See Also
78|    ========
79|

82|    Examples
83|    ========
84|
85|    >>> from sympy.geometry import Point
86|    >>> from sympy.abc import x
87|    >>> Point(1, 2, 3)
88|    Point3D(1, 2, 3)
89|    >>> Point([1, 2])
90|    Point2D(1, 2)
91|    >>> Point(0, x)
92|    Point2D(0, x)
93|    >>> Point(dim=4)
94|    Point(0, 0, 0, 0)
95|
96|    Floats are automatically converted to Rational unless the
97|    evaluate flag is False:
98|
99|    >>> Point(0.5, 0.25)
100|    Point2D(1/2, 1/4)
101|    >>> Point(0.5, 0.25, evaluate=False)
102|    Point2D(0.5, 0.25)
103|
104|    """
105|
106|    is_Point = True
107|
108|    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
109|        evaluate = kwargs.get('evaluate', global_evaluate[0])
110|        on_morph = kwargs.get('on_morph', 'ignore')
111|
112|        # unpack into coords
113|        coords = args[0] if len(args) == 1 else args
114|
115|        # check args and handle quickly handle Point instances
116|        if isinstance(coords, Point):
117|            # even if we're mutating the dimension of a point, we
118|            # don't reevaluate its coordinates
119|            evaluate = False
120|            if len(coords) == kwargs.get('dim', len(coords)):
121|                return coords
122|
123|        if not is_sequence(coords):
124|            raise TypeError(filldedent('''
125|                Expecting sequence of coordinates, not `{}`'''
126|                                       .format(func_name(coords))))
127|        # A point where only `dim` is specified is initialized
128|        # to zeros.
129|        if len(coords) == 0 and kwargs.get('dim', None):
130|            coords = (S.Zero,)*kwargs.get('dim')
131|
132|        coords = Tuple(*coords)
133|        dim = kwargs.get('dim', len(coords))
134|
135|        if len(coords) < 2:
136|            raise ValueError(filldedent('''
137|                Point requires 2 or more coordinates or
138|                keyword `dim` > 1.'''))
139|        if len(coords) != dim:
140|            message = ("Dimension of {} needs to be changed "
141|                       "from {} to {}.").format(coords, len(coords), dim)
142|            if on_morph == 'ignore':
143|                pass
144|            elif on_morph == "error":
145|                raise ValueError(message)
146|            elif on_morph == 'warn':
147|                warnings.warn(message)
148|            else:
149|                raise ValueError(filldedent('''
150|                        on_morph value should be 'error',
151|                        'warn' or 'ignore'.'''))
152|        if any(coords[dim:]):
153|            raise ValueError('Nonzero coordinates cannot be removed.')
154|        if any(a.is_number and im(a) for a in coords):
155|            raise ValueError('Imaginary coordinates are not permitted.')
156|        if not all(isinstance(a, Expr) for a in coords):
157|            raise TypeError('Coordinates must be valid SymPy expressions.')
158|
159|        # pad with zeros appropriately
160|        coords = coords[:dim] + (S.Zero,)*(dim - len(coords))
161|
162|        # Turn any Floats into rationals and simplify
163|        # any expressions before we instantiate
164|        if evaluate:
165|            coords = coords.xreplace(dict(
166|                [(f, simplify(nsimplify(f, rational=True)))
167|                 for f in coords.atoms(Float)]))
168|
169|        # return 2D or 3D instances
170|        if len(coords) == 2:
171|            kwargs['_nocheck'] = True
172|            return Point2D(*coords, **kwargs)
173|        elif len(coords) == 3:
174|            kwargs['_nocheck'] = True
175|            return Point3D(*coords, **kwargs)
176|
177|        # the general Point
178|        return GeometryEntity.__new__(cls, *coords)

185|    def __add__(self, other):
186|        """Add other to self by incrementing self's coordinates by
187|        those of other.
188|
189|        Notes
190|        =====
191|
192|        >>> from sympy.geometry.point import Point
193|
194|        When sequences of coordinates are passed to Point methods, they
195|        are converted to a Point internally. This __add__ method does
196|        not do that so if floating point values are used, a floating
197|        point result (in terms of SymPy Floats) will be returned.
198|
199|        >>> Point(1, 2) + (.1, .2)
200|        Point2D(1.1, 2.2)
201|
202|        If this is not desired, the `translate` method can be used or
203|        another Point can be added:
204|
205|        >>> Point(1, 2).translate(.1, .2)
206|        Point2D(11/10, 11/5)
207|        >>> Point(1, 2) + Point(.1, .2)
208|        Point2D(11/10, 11/5)

210|        See Also
211|        ========
212|
213|        sympy.geometry.point.Point.translate

215|        """
216|        try:
217|            s, o = Point._normalize_dimension(self, Point(other, evaluate=False))
218|        except TypeError:
219|            raise GeometryError("Don't know how to add {} and a Point object".format(other))
220|
221|        coords = [simplify(a + b) for a, b in zip(s, o)]
222|        return Point(coords, evaluate=False)

291|    @classmethod
292|    def _normalize_dimension(cls, *points, **kwargs):
293|        """Ensure that points have the same dimension.
294|        By default `on_morph='warn'` is passed to the
295|        `Point` constructor."""
296|        # if we have a built-in ambient dimension, use it
297|        dim = getattr(cls, '_ambient_dimension', None)
298|        # override if we specified it
299|        dim = kwargs.get('dim', dim)
300|        # if no dim was given, use the highest dimensional point
301|        if dim is None:
302|            dim = max(i.ambient_dimension for i in points)
303|        if all(i.ambient_dimension == dim for i in points):
304|            return list(points)
305|        kwargs['dim'] = dim
306|        kwargs['on_morph'] = kwargs.get('on_morph', 'warn')
307|        return [Point(i, **kwargs) for i in points]

309|    @staticmethod
310|    def affine_rank(*args):
311|        """The affine rank of a set of points is the dimension
312|        of the smallest affine space containing all the points.
313|        For example, if the points lie on a line (and are not all
314|        the same) their affine rank is 1.  If the points lie on a plane
315|        but not a line, their affine rank is 2.  By convention, the empty
316|        set has affine rank -1."""
317|
318|        if len(args) == 0:
319|            return -1
320|        # make sure we're genuinely points
321|        # and translate every point to the origin
322|        points = Point._normalize_dimension(*[Point(i) for i in args])
323|        origin = points[0]
324|        points = [i - origin for i in points[1:]]
325|
326|        m = Matrix([i.args for i in points])
327|        # XXX fragile -- what is a better way?
328|        return m.rank(iszerofunc = lambda x:
329|            abs(x.n(2)) < 1e-12 if x.is_number else x.is_zero)
330|
331|    @property
332|    def ambient_dimension(self):
333|        """Number of components this point has."""
334|        return getattr(self, '_ambient_dimension', len(self))

336|    @classmethod
337|    def are_coplanar(cls, *points):
338|        """Return True if there exists a plane in which all the points
339|        lie.  A trivial True value is returned if `len(points) < 3` or
340|        all Points are 2-dimensional.
341|
342|        Parameters
343|        ==========
344|
345|        A set of points
346|
347|        Raises
348|        ======
349|
350|        ValueError : if less than 3 unique points are given
351|
352|        Returns
353|        =======
354|
355|        boolean
356|
357|        Examples
358|        ========
359|
360|        >>> from sympy import Point3D
361|        >>> p1 = Point3D(1, 2, 2)
362|        >>> p2 = Point3D(2, 7, 2)
363|        >>> p3 = Point3D(0, 0, 2)
364|        >>> p4 = Point3D(1, 1, 2)
365|        >>> Point3D.are_coplanar(p1, p2, p3, p4)
366|        True
367|        >>> p5 = Point3D(0, 1, 3)
368|        >>> Point3D.are_coplanar(p1, p2, p3, p5)
369|        False
370|
371|        """
372|        if len(points) <= 1:
373|            return True
374|
375|        points = cls._normalize_dimension(*[Point(i) for i in points])
376|        # quick exit if we are in 2D
377|        if points[0].ambient_dimension == 2:
378|            return True
379|        points = list(uniq(points))
380|        return Point.affine_rank(*points) <= 2

382|    def distance(self, other):
383|        """The Euclidean distance between self and another GeometricEntity.
384|
385|        Returns
386|        =======
387|
388|        distance : number or symbolic expression.
389|
390|        Raises
391|        ======
392|
393|        TypeError : if other is not recognized as a GeometricEntity or is a
394|                    GeometricEntity for which distance is not defined.
395|
396|        See Also
397|        ========
398|
399|        sympy.geometry.line.Segment.length
400|        sympy.geometry.point.Point.taxicab_distance
401|
402|        Examples
403|        ========
404|
405|        >>> from sympy.geometry import Point, Line
406|        >>> p1, p2 = Point(1, 1), Point(4, 5)
407|        >>> l = Line((3, 1), (2, 2))
408|        >>> p1.distance(p2)
409|        5
410|        >>> p1.distance(l)
411|        sqrt(2)
412|
413|        The computed distance may be symbolic, too:
414|
415|        >>> from sympy.abc import x, y
416|        >>> p3 = Point(x, y)
417|        >>> p3.distance((0, 0))
418|        sqrt(x**2 + y**2)
419|
420|        """
421|        if not isinstance(other, GeometryEntity):
422|            try:
423|                other = Point(other, dim=self.ambient_dimension)
424|            except TypeError:
425|                raise TypeError("not recognized as a GeometricEntity: %s" % type(other))
426|        if isinstance(other, Point):
427|            s, p = Point._normalize_dimension(self, Point(other))
428|            return sqrt(Add(*((a - b)**2 for a, b in zip(s, p))))
429|        distance = getattr(other, 'distance', None)
430|        if distance is None:
431|            raise TypeError("distance between Point and %s is not defined" % type(other))
432|        return distance(self)

436|        if not is_sequence(p):
437|            p = Point(p)  # raise the error via Point
438|        return Add(*(a*b for a, b in zip(self, p)))

442|        # a point is equal to another point if all its components are equal
443|        if not isinstance(other, Point) or len(self) != len(other):
444|            return False

478|    def intersection(self, other):
479|        """The intersection between this point and another GeometryEntity.

484|        other : GeometryEntity or sequence of coordinates

487|        =======

492|        =====

495|        intersection, otherwise it will contain this point.

498|        ========

500|        >>> from sympy import Point
501|        >>> p1, p2, p3 = Point(0, 0), Point(1, 1), Point(0, 0)
502|        >>> p1.intersection(p2)
503|        []
504|        >>> p1.intersection(p3)
505|        [Point2D(0, 0)]

507|        """
508|        if not isinstance(other, GeometryEntity):
509|            other = Point(other)
510|        if isinstance(other, Point):
511|            if self == other:
512|                return [self]
513|            p1, p2 = Point._normalize_dimension(self, other)
514|            if p1 == self and p1 == p2:
515|                return [self]
516|            return []

519|    def is_collinear(self, *args):
520|        """Returns `True` if there exists a line
521|        that contains `self` and `points`.  Returns `False` otherwise.
522|        A trivially True value is returned if no points are given.
523|

525|        ==========

530|        =======

535|        ========

540|        ========

545|        >>> p3, p4, p5 = Point(2, 2), Point(x, x), Point(1, 2)
546|        >>> Point.is_collinear(p1, p2, p3, p4)
547|        True

557|    def is_concyclic(self, *args):
558|        """Do `self` and the given sequence of points lie in a circle?
559|
560|        Returns True if the set of points are concyclic and
561|        False otherwise. A trivial value of True is returned
562|        if there are fewer than 2 other points.
563|
564|        Parameters
565|        ==========
566|
567|        args : sequence of Points
568|
569|        Returns
570|        =======
571|
572|        is_concyclic : boolean
573|
574|
575|        Examples
576|        ========
577|
578|        >>> from sympy import Point
579|
580|        Define 4 points that are on the unit circle:
581|
582|        >>> p1, p2, p3, p4 = Point(1, 0), (0, 1), (-1, 0), (0, -1)
583|
584|        >>> p1.is_concyclic() == p1.is_concyclic(p2, p3, p4) == True
585|        True
586|
587|        Define a point not on that circle:
588|
589|        >>> p = Point(1, 1)
590|
591|        >>> p.is_concyclic(p1, p2, p3)
592|        False
593|
594|        """
595|        points = (self,) + args
596|        points = Point._normalize_dimension(*[Point(i) for i in points])
597|        points = list(uniq(points))
598|        if not Point.affine_rank(*points) <= 2:
599|            return False
600|        origin = points[0]
601|        points = [p - origin for p in points]
602|        # points are concyclic if they are coplanar and
603|        # there is a point c so that ||p_i-c|| == ||p_j-c|| for all
604|        # i and j.  Rearranging this equation gives us the following
605|        # condition: the matrix `mat` must not a pivot in the last
606|        # column.
607|        mat = Matrix([list(i) + [i.dot(i)] for i in points])
608|        rref, pivots = mat.rref()
609|        if len(origin) not in pivots:
610|            return True
611|        return False

622|    def is_scalar_multiple(self, p):
623|        """Returns whether each coordinate of `self` is a scalar
624|        multiple of the corresponding coordinate in point p.
625|        """
626|        s, o = Point._normalize_dimension(self, Point(p))
627|        # 2d points happen a lot, so optimize this function call
628|        if s.ambient_dimension == 2:
629|            (x1, y1), (x2, y2) = s.args, o.args
630|            rv = (x1*y2 - x2*y1).equals(0)
631|            if rv is None:
632|                raise Undecidable(filldedent(
633|                    '''can't determine if %s is a scalar multiple of
634|                    %s''' % (s, o)))
635|
636|        # if the vectors p1 and p2 are linearly dependent, then they must
637|        # be scalar multiples of each other
638|        m = Matrix([s.args, o.args])
639|        return m.rank() < 2

646|        if any(nonzero):
647|            return False
648|        if any(x is None for x in nonzero):
649|            return None
650|        return True

703|    @property
704|    def orthogonal_direction(self):
705|        """Returns a non-zero point that is orthogonal to the
706|        line containing `self` and the origin.
707|
708|        Examples
709|        ========
710|
711|        >>> from sympy.geometry import Line, Point
712|        >>> a = Point(1, 2, 3)
713|        >>> a.orthogonal_direction
714|        Point3D(-2, 1, 0)
715|        >>> b = _
716|        >>> Line(b, b.origin).is_perpendicular(Line(a, a.origin))
717|        True
718|        """
719|        dim = self.ambient_dimension
720|        # if a coordinate is zero, we can put a 1 there and zeros elsewhere
721|        if self[0].is_zero:
722|            return Point([1] + (dim - 1)*[0])
723|        if self[1].is_zero:
724|            return Point([0,1] + (dim - 2)*[0])
725|        # if the first two coordinates aren't zero, we can create a non-zero
726|        # orthogonal vector by swapping them, negating one, and padding with zeros
727|        return Point([-self[1], self[0]] + (dim - 2)*[0])

583|        is done only if ``wrt`` is different than the free symbols.
584|
585|        2) differentiation with respect to variables in 'wrt' (or all free
586|        symbols if omitted) to see if the expression is constant or not. This
587|        will not always lead to an expression that is zero even though an
588|        expression is constant (see added test in test_expr.py). If
589|        all derivatives are zero then self is constant with respect to the
590|        given symbols.
591|
592|        If neither evaluation nor differentiation can prove the expression is
593|        constant, None is returned unless two numerical values happened to be
594|        the same and the flag ``failing_number`` is True -- in that case the
595|        numerical value will be returned.
596|
597|        If flag simplify=False is passed, self will not be simplified;
598|        the default is True since self should be simplified before testing.
599|
600|        Examples
601|        ========
602|
603|        >>> from sympy import cos, sin, Sum, S, pi
604|        >>> from sympy.abc import a, n, x, y
605|        >>> x.is_constant()
606|        False
607|        >>> S(2).is_constant()
608|        True
609|        >>> Sum(x, (x, 1, 10)).is_constant()
610|        True
611|        >>> Sum(x, (x, 1, n)).is_constant()
612|        False
613|        >>> Sum(x, (x, 1, n)).is_constant(y)
614|        True
615|        >>> Sum(x, (x, 1, n)).is_constant(n)
616|        False
617|        >>> Sum(x, (x, 1, n)).is_constant(x)
618|        True
619|        >>> eq = a*cos(x)**2 + a*sin(x)**2 - a
620|        >>> eq.is_constant()
621|        True
622|        >>> eq.subs({x: pi, a: 2}) == eq.subs({x: pi, a: 3}) == 0
623|        True
624|
625|        >>> (0**x).is_constant()
626|        False
627|        >>> x.is_constant()
628|        False
629|        >>> (x**x).is_constant()
630|        False
631|        >>> one = cos(x)**2 + sin(x)**2
632|        >>> one.is_constant()
633|        True
634|        >>> ((one - 1)**(x + 1)).is_constant() in (True, False) # could be 0 or 1
635|        True
636|        """
637|
638|        simplify = flags.get('simplify', True)
639|
640|        if self.is_number:
641|            return True
642|        free = self.free_symbols
643|        if not free:
644|            return True  # assume f(1) is some constant
645|
646|        # if we are only interested in some symbols and they are not in the
647|        # free symbols then this expression is constant wrt those symbols
648|        wrt = set(wrt)
649|        if wrt and not wrt & free:
650|            return True
651|        wrt = wrt or free
652|
653|        # simplify unless this has already been done
654|        expr = self
655|        if simplify:
656|            expr = expr.simplify()
657|
658|        # is_zero should be a quick assumptions check; it can be wrong for
659|        # numbers (see test_is_not_constant test), giving False when it
660|        # shouldn't, but hopefully it will never give True unless it is sure.
661|        if expr.is_zero:
662|            return True
663|
664|        # try numerical evaluation to see if we get two different values
665|        failing_number = None
666|        if wrt == free:
667|            # try 0 (for a) and 1 (for b)
668|            try:
669|                a = expr.subs(list(zip(free, [0]*len(free))),
670|                    simultaneous=True)
671|                if a is S.NaN:
672|                    # evaluation may succeed when substitution fails
673|                    a = expr._random(None, 0, 0, 0, 0)
674|            except ZeroDivisionError:
675|                a = None
676|            if a is not None and a is not S.NaN:
677|                try:
678|                    b = expr.subs(list(zip(free, [1]*len(free))),
679|                        simultaneous=True)
680|                    if b is S.NaN:
681|                        # evaluation may succeed when substitution fails
682|                        b = expr._random(None, 1, 0, 1, 0)
683|                except ZeroDivisionError:
684|                    b = None
685|                if b is not None and b is not S.NaN and b.equals(a) is False:
686|                    return False
687|                # try random real
688|                b = expr._random(None, -1, 0, 1, 0)
689|                if b is not None and b is not S.NaN and b.equals(a) is False:
690|                    return False
691|                # try random complex
692|                b = expr._random()
693|                if b is not None and b is not S.NaN:
694|                    if b.equals(a) is False:
695|                        return False
696|                    failing_number = a if a.is_number else b
697|
698|        # now we will test each wrt symbol (or all free symbols) to see if the
699|        # expression depends on them or not using differentiation. This is
700|        # not sufficient for all expressions, however, so we don't return
701|        # False if we get a derivative other than 0 with free symbols.
702|        for w in wrt:
703|            deriv = expr.diff(w)
704|            if simplify:
705|                deriv = deriv.simplify()
706|            if deriv != 0:
707|                if not (pure_complex(deriv, or_real=True)):
708|                    if flags.get('failing_number', False):
709|                        return failing_number
710|                    elif deriv.free_symbols:
711|                        # dead line provided _random returns None in such cases
712|                        return None
713|                return False
714|        return True

716|    def equals(self, other, failing_expression=False):
717|        """Return True if self == other, False if it doesn't, or None. If
718|        failing_expression is True then the expression which did not simplify
719|        to a 0 will be returned instead of None.
720|
721|        If ``self`` is a Number (or complex number) that is not zero, then
722|        the result is False.
723|
724|        If ``self`` is a number and has not evaluated to zero, evalf will be
725|        used to test whether the expression evaluates to zero. If it does so
726|        and the result has significance (i.e. the precision is either -1, for
727|        a Rational result, or is greater than 1) then the evalf value will be
728|        used to return True or False.
729|
730|        """
731|        from sympy.simplify.simplify import nsimplify, simplify
732|        from sympy.solvers.solveset import solveset
733|        from sympy.solvers.solvers import solve
734|        from sympy.polys.polyerrors import NotAlgebraic
735|        from sympy.polys.numberfields import minimal_polynomial
736|
737|        other = sympify(other)
738|        if self == other:
739|            return True
740|
741|        # they aren't the same so see if we can make the difference 0;
742|        # don't worry about doing simplification steps one at a time
743|        # because if the expression ever goes to 0 then the subsequent
744|        # simplification steps that are done will be very fast.
745|        diff = factor_terms(simplify(self - other), radical=True)
746|
747|        if not diff:
748|            return True
749|
750|        if not diff.has(Add, Mod):
751|            # if there is no expanding to be done after simplifying
752|            # then this can't be a zero
753|            return False
754|
755|        constant = diff.is_constant(simplify=False, failing_number=True)
756|
757|        if constant is False:
758|            return False
759|
760|        if not diff.is_number:
761|            if constant is None:
762|                # e.g. unless the right simplification is done, a symbolic
763|                # zero is possible (see expression of issue 6829: without
764|                # simplification constant will be None).
765|                return
766|
767|        if constant is True:
768|            # this gives a number whether there are free symbols or not
769|            ndiff = diff._random()
770|            # is_comparable will work whether the result is real
771|            # or complex; it could be None, however.
772|            if ndiff and ndiff.is_comparable:
773|                return False
774|
775|        # sometimes we can use a simplified result to give a clue as to
776|        # what the expression should be; if the expression is *not* zero
777|        # then we should have been able to compute that and so now
778|        # we can just consider the cases where the approximation appears
779|        # to be zero -- we try to prove it via minimal_polynomial.
780|        #
781|        # removed
782|        # ns = nsimplify(diff)
783|        # if diff.is_number and (not ns or ns == diff):
784|        #
785|        # The thought was that if it nsimplifies to 0 that's a sure sign
786|        # to try the following to prove it; or if it changed but wasn't
787|        # zero that might be a sign that it's not going to be easy to
788|        # prove. But tests seem to be working without that logic.
789|        #
790|        if diff.is_number:
791|            # try to prove via self-consistency
792|            surds = [s for s in diff.atoms(Pow) if s.args[0].is_Integer]
793|            # it seems to work better to try big ones first
794|            surds.sort(key=lambda x: -x.args[0])
795|            for s in surds:
796|                try:
797|                    # simplify is False here -- this expression has already
798|                    # been identified as being hard to identify as zero;
799|                    # we will handle the checking ourselves using nsimplify
800|                    # to see if we are in the right ballpark or not and if so
801|                    # *then* the simplification will be attempted.
802|                    sol = solve(diff, s, simplify=False)
803|                    if sol:
804|                        if s in sol:
805|                            # the self-consistent result is present
806|                            return True
807|                        if all(si.is_Integer for si in sol):
808|                            # perfect powers are removed at instantiation
809|                            # so surd s cannot be an integer
810|                            return False
811|                        if all(i.is_algebraic is False for i in sol):
812|                            # a surd is algebraic
813|                            return False
814|                        if any(si in surds for si in sol):
815|                            # it wasn't equal to s but it is in surds
816|                            # and different surds are not equal
817|                            return False
818|                        if any(nsimplify(s - si) == 0 and
819|                                simplify(s - si) == 0 for si in sol):
820|                            return True
821|                        if s.is_real:
822|                            if any(nsimplify(si, [s]) == s and simplify(si) == s
823|                                    for si in sol):
824|                                return True
825|                except NotImplementedError:
826|                    pass
827|
828|            # try to prove with minimal_polynomial but know when
829|            # *not* to use this or else it can take a long time. e.g. issue 8354
830|            if True:  # change True to condition that assures non-hang
831|                try:
832|                    mp = minimal_polynomial(diff)
833|                    if mp.is_Symbol:
834|                        return True
835|                    return False
836|                except (NotAlgebraic, NotImplementedError):
837|                    pass
838|
839|        # diff has not simplified to zero; constant is either None, True
840|        # or the number with significance (is_comparable) that was randomly
841|        # calculated twice as the same value.
842|        if constant not in (True, None) and constant != 0:
843|            return False
844|
845|        if failing_expression:
846|            return diff
847|        return None

939|    def _eval_interval(self, x, a, b):
940|        """
941|        Returns evaluation over an interval.  For most functions this is:
942|
943|        self.subs(x, b) - self.subs(x, a),
944|
945|        possibly using limit() if NaN is returned from subs, or if
946|        singularities are found between a and b.
947|
948|        If b or a is None, it only evaluates -self.subs(x, a) or self.subs(b, x),
949|        respectively.
950|
951|        """
952|        from sympy.series import limit, Limit
953|        from sympy.solvers.solveset import solveset
954|        from sympy.sets.sets import Interval
955|        from sympy.functions.elementary.exponential import log
956|        from sympy.calculus.util import AccumBounds
957|
958|        if (a is None and b is None):
959|            raise ValueError('Both interval ends cannot be None.')
960|
961|        if a == b:
962|            return 0
963|
964|        if a is None:
965|            A = 0
966|        else:
967|            A = self.subs(x, a)
968|            if A.has(S.NaN, S.Infinity, S.NegativeInfinity, S.ComplexInfinity, AccumBounds):
969|                if (a < b) != False:
970|                    A = limit(self, x, a,"+")
971|                else:
972|                    A = limit(self, x, a,"-")
973|
974|                if A is S.NaN:
975|                    return A
976|                if isinstance(A, Limit):
977|                    raise NotImplementedError("Could not compute limit")
978|
979|        if b is None:
980|            B = 0
981|        else:
982|            B = self.subs(x, b)
983|            if B.has(S.NaN, S.Infinity, S.NegativeInfinity, S.ComplexInfinity, AccumBounds):
984|                if (a < b) != False:
985|                    B = limit(self, x, b,"-")
986|                else:
987|                    B = limit(self, x, b,"+")
988|
989|                if isinstance(B, Limit):
990|                    raise NotImplementedError("Could not compute limit")
991|
992|        if (a and b) is None:
993|            return B - A
994|
995|        value = B - A
996|
997|        if a.is_comparable and b.is_comparable:
998|            if a < b:
999|                domain = Interval(a, b)
1000|            else:
1001|                domain = Interval(b, a)
1002|            # check the singularities of self within the interval
1003|            # if singularities is a ConditionSet (not iterable), catch the exception and pass
1004|            singularities = solveset(self.cancel().as_numer_denom()[1], x,
1005|                domain=domain)
1006|            for logterm in self.atoms(log):
1007|                singularities = singularities | solveset(logterm.args[0], x,
1008|                    domain=domain)
1009|            try:
1010|                for s in singularities:
1011|                    if value is S.NaN:
1012|                        # no need to keep adding, it will stay NaN
1013|                        break
1014|                    if not s.is_comparable:
1015|                        continue
1016|                    if (a < s) == (s < b) == True:
1017|                        value += -limit(self, x, s, "+") + limit(self, x, s, "-")
1018|                    elif (b < s) == (s < a) == True:
1019|                        value += limit(self, x, s, "+") - limit(self, x, s, "-")
1020|            except TypeError:
1021|                pass
1022|
1023|        return value

1130|            # first number positive and thhe second number nagative

1133|            if (len(add_args) == 2

1137|                if (len(mul_args) == 2

1139|                    and add_args[0].is_positive
1140|                    and mul_args[0].is_negative):

1229|    def getn(self):
1230|        """
1231|        Returns the order of the expression.
1232|
1233|        The order is determined either from the O(...) term. If there
1234|        is no O(...) term, it returns None.
1235|
1236|        Examples
1237|        ========
1238|
1239|        >>> from sympy import O
1240|        >>> from sympy.abc import x
1241|        >>> (1 + x + O(x**2)).getn()
1242|        2
1243|        >>> (1 + x).getn()
1244|
1245|        """
1246|        from sympy import Dummy, Symbol
1247|        o = self.getO()
1248|        if o is None:
1249|            return None
1250|        elif o.is_Order:
1251|            o = o.expr
1252|            if o is S.One:
1253|                return S.Zero
1254|            if o.is_Symbol:
1255|                return S.One
1256|            if o.is_Pow:
1257|                return o.args[1]
1258|            if o.is_Mul:  # x**n*log(x)**n or x**n/log(x)**n
1259|                for oi in o.args:
1260|                    if oi.is_Symbol:
1261|                        return S.One
1262|                    if oi.is_Pow:
1263|                        syms = oi.atoms(Symbol)
1264|                        if len(syms) == 1:
1265|                            x = syms.pop()
1266|                            oi = oi.subs(x, Dummy('x', positive=True))
1267|                            if oi.base.is_Symbol and oi.exp.is_Rational:
1268|                                return abs(oi.exp)
1269|
